data.objective: B2 Word Formation: building meaning in context
data.learn: In Part 3, the gap needs a form of the supplied word. Read the whole sentence to decide its grammatical role, then check number, negative meaning and spelling. Suffixes are clues, not rules that work for every word. A noun may require a plural ending; an adjective may need a negative prefix. Read the finished paragraph to ensure the meaning fits.

worked.example: The route is not SAFE in winter → Safety depends on the weather.
worked.reasoning: The first gap would need “safe”; after a verb such as “depends”, the subject needs the noun “safety”. Meaning and syntax determine the form.

tasks.title: Guided task planning
tasks.instructions: Write 50–80 words planning the independent Write an Email task below. Identify the reader or discussion issue, the required points and the order you would use. Do not compose the full response yet.

tasks.title: Independent Write an Email
tasks.instructions: You are preparing a group presentation. The assigned room’s projector does not work. Write to your instructor: explain the problem, propose an alternative, and ask for a decision. Include enough detail for the instructor to respond. Local practice target: 120–180 words in seven minutes.
tasks.model:
Dear Dr Chen,

I am writing about the presentation scheduled for Thursday. Our group has completed the research, but the projector in the assigned room is not working. We tested it this morning and could not display our slides, even with a different laptop.

Would it be possible to move the presentation to room 12? The room is listed as available at the same time, and its screen worked during our last seminar. If changing rooms is not possible, we can prepare printed copies of the key charts, although this would make the demonstration less clear.

Please let us know which option you prefer so that we can inform the other students and prepare the appropriate materials. We are available to test the equipment again before class if that would help.

Thank you for your advice.

Best regards,
Sam Malik

tasks.title: Assessment: a fresh email
tasks.instructions: You organise a student photography exhibition. A room booking confirmation gives the wrong date: 18 March rather than 25 March. Email the campus events officer. Explain the error and why it matters, request the correct date or a suitable alternative, and ask how to confirm the amended booking.
tasks.model:
Dear Events Officer,

I am writing about the room confirmation for our student photography exhibition. Our group requested 25 March, but the confirmation lists 18 March. Several contributors will be away on that earlier date, so we could not display their work.

Could you check whether the room is available on 25 March and amend the booking? If it has already been reserved, a similar space on the same afternoon would be helpful. We need room for twelve display boards and expect about thirty visitors.

Please let me know which option is possible and whether I need to submit a new form. I can send our original request immediately if that would help you locate the correct booking.

Kind regards,
Alex

tasks.title: Independent Academic Discussion development
tasks.instructions: Professor: Should a university spend limited funds on longer library opening hours or more online resources? Noah favours longer hours for quiet study. Priya favours digital access for commuting students. Contribute an original, supported view that responds to the discussion. Aim for at least 100 words.
tasks.model: Priya’s point about commuting students is important, but I would first identify which barrier affects the largest number of users. More online resources will not solve the problem for students who lack a quiet place to work, while longer opening hours may be unhelpful if transport stops early. I would use a short survey and existing access records to compare these needs. The university could then trial one later evening alongside remote access to a small set of frequently requested materials. This would produce evidence before committing the whole budget. The choice should follow actual learning needs rather than assuming that either physical or digital access is always superior.

tasks.title: Assessment: a fresh academic discussion
tasks.instructions: Professor: A university is considering replacing some large lectures with small workshops. Sara believes workshops make participation easier. Ben worries that fewer lectures would reduce access to expert explanations. What arrangement would you recommend? Engage with a viewpoint and explain your reasoning. Aim for at least 100 words.
tasks.model: I would retain a shorter expert lecture and use the remaining time for small workshops. Sara is right that students need opportunities to test their understanding rather than only listen. In a workshop, they could explain an answer to a partner and discover which step they have misunderstood. However, Ben identifies a real risk: students may struggle if they are asked to solve problems before the key concepts have been explained. A short lecture could introduce those concepts, while a prepared workshop task would require students to apply them. Tutors could collect common difficulties and pass them back to the lecturer. This would connect explanation and participation rather than make them competing priorities.
rubric: I recommend a specific arrangement, not simply list advantages.
I respond to Sara or Ben and explain an example of learning.
I use a natural academic discussion register and check clarity.
I checked language, connections and punctuation.
tasks.analysis: Trace each requested point in the model, then compare how your response fulfils it. These are original teaching models for self-review, not examiner-rated scripts.

tasks.title: Independent Timed Email and Discussion transfer
tasks.instructions: Professor: Should first-year students choose all their courses, or follow a partly required programme? Elise favours freedom; David argues that beginners need guidance. Contribute your position and engage with at least one viewpoint. Aim for at least 100 words.
tasks.model: I support a partly required programme because first-year students may not yet know which foundations later courses assume. David is right that guidance can prevent choices that close useful opportunities. However, Elise’s concern about motivation also matters: students should have room to explore a subject that interests them. A small required core combined with several elective options would balance these needs. Advisers could explain the purpose of each requirement rather than presenting it as an arbitrary restriction. After the first year, students would have more experience on which to base independent choices. This approach provides support without treating all learners as if they have identical goals.

tasks.title: Assessment: a fresh email
tasks.instructions: You are helping organise a campus careers event. A guest speaker has asked for an online connection, but the assigned room has no video-call equipment. Email the careers adviser. Explain the difficulty, propose a practical solution, and request a decision before you contact the speaker. Local practice target: 120–180 words in seven minutes.
tasks.model:
Dear Careers Adviser,

I am contacting you about Thursday’s careers event. Our guest speaker has asked to join online because her train has been cancelled. Unfortunately, Room 14 has no camera or speakers suitable for a video call, so the current arrangement will not allow the audience to hear her properly.

Could we move the session to the language laboratory? It has the necessary equipment and is free after three, according to the booking calendar. I could help test the connection with the technician before the event. If that room cannot be reserved, another option would be to hold the interview online and send students a joining link.

Please let me know which arrangement you approve by tomorrow afternoon. I will wait for your decision before confirming anything with the speaker.

Kind regards,
Jamie

I propose a feasible solution with useful practical details.
